title: People who care
subject: RSHE

thread_tags.line: Thread tags: SMSC S/M/So (C: none); British Values IL/MR (D/RL/T: none).
thread_tags.rationale: S: reflect on a fictional person’s needs and choices. M: consider caring and helpful actions. So: listen to different possible responses. IL: respect a choice to pause or use a response aid. MR: respect different families and feelings without ranking people.

label: Public edition
objective_verbatim: Recognise caring relationships and identify an action that shows care.
display_objective: Spot a caring act that helps a young person.
approved_activity: Explore fictional family and caring-role cards, recognising that families can look different.
Match caring actions to situations and build a support map for a fictional young person.
calendar_note: Year A. 2–6 November 2026. One 40-minute lesson. No day or clock slot inferred. Week 7 is assessing.
where_this_leads: This helps me recognise respectful support from people I learn or work with.
unit: Caring relationships, feelings and helpful responses
accreditation: The qualification and the accredited unit: staff confirm any mapping from actual work. No criteria or completion are inferred.
assessment: Weeks 1–6 are formative. Week 7 is the assessing lesson. Keep actual responses, support, gaps and next steps in the evidence record.

sources.note: The owner-approved standalone RSHE outline is the weekly teaching source. The three build notes apply throughout. No separate workbook row is asserted.

authoring_provenance.note: Newly authored tasks from the owner-approved RSHE outline. No separate weekly workbook row is asserted. All prompts use fictional cases.

external_sources.note: Approval, curriculum context, template and authored visual provenance.

evidence.description: A caring-action match and a fictional support map, with the learner’s explanation and support recorded.
evidence.status: not prefilled; actual response and support to be recorded

routes.Supported: Supported: use two caring-action choices, then make a support map with two supplied role cards and reading or scribing support.
routes.Independent: Independent: match three caring actions and build the fictional support map, giving one reason from a card.
routes.Aspire: Aspire: explain why a helpful action respects choice and add a second help route if the first adult is unavailable.

vocab.definition: Help keep a person safe and well.
People linked by care or birth.
Hear what a person has to say.
An option a person can pick.
Feel able to ask a person for help.
Help a person with a need.

cases.text: A young person needs time to talk.
cases.next_step: Caring action: the adult lets the person finish and checks what help is wanted.

cases.text: A young person is stuck on a task.
cases.next_step: Caring action: help with the stated need, without taking over every choice.

cases.text: A young person asks for some space.
cases.judgement: Give space and stay ready to help.
cases.next_step: Caring action: respect space; no forced touch or demand for a private reason.

cases.text: A young person asks a question. An adult laughs.
cases.judgement: Not a caring response in this story.
cases.next_step: Replace laughter with listening and a useful reply.

cases.text: A young person wants to choose. An adult picks every time.
cases.judgement: This does not respect their choice.
cases.next_step: Ask what help is wanted and offer a supported choice.

cases.text: A young person needs help. The first adult is busy.
cases.next_step: The support map supplies a tutor and a support adult. Keep the request available for a follow-up.

RSHE-BUILD-A2-W01 · Year A · Week beginning 2 November 2026
Term theme: Identity & Belonging
Thread tags: SMSC S/M/So (C: none); British Values IL/MR (D/RL/T: none).
Staff brief: 0 minutes.
Teacher: Every teaching prompt concerns a fictional young person. Never ask learners about their own bodies, families or experiences, or use a real person as the case. Read fictional cards without inviting comparison with home. No touching, body checking, forced eye contact, acting out distress or personal role-play. Allow a pass, quiet response or pause. If a learner raises a personal concern, follow the setting’s safeguarding procedure; do not turn the disclosure into lesson evidence. Staff use the setting’s agreed support arrangements.
Routes: Supported: use two caring-action choices, then make a support map with two supplied role cards and reading or scribing support. Independent: match three caring actions and build the fictional support map, giving one reason from a card. Aspire: explain why a helpful action respects choice and add a second help route if the first adult is unavailable.
Evidence: A caring-action match and a fictional support map, with the learner’s explanation and support recorded.
Careers: This helps me recognise respectful support from people I learn or work with.

A is supported by the caring action. B is unkind. C removes choice rather than checking what help is wanted. An adult’s role alone does not prove that an action is caring. Reteach with the card about waiting while a person speaks; ask what that action allows.

Supported: use two caring-action choices, then make a support map with two supplied role cards and reading or scribing support. Independent: match three caring actions and build the fictional support map, giving one reason from a card. Aspire: explain why a helpful action respects choice and add a second help route if the first adult is unavailable.

Use four minutes to match caring actions to fictional situations. Use five minutes to make a support map for the supplied young person using the tutor and support-adult cards. Use three minutes to explain one caring action and consider the next help route if the first adult is busy. Preserve the first response and any prompted change.
Read aloud, point, scribe exact words or use the usual communication aid. Record support without treating speech speed or handwriting as the target.

Record the actual situation and caring-action match, a map linking the fictional young person to at least one appropriate support role, and the learner’s explanation. R requires Voice, Audience, a specific NS+ prompt and the learner response in their own colour. E is recorded only when actual work is banked. Record prompts and unfinished work. Blank sheets and adult models are not completed learner evidence.

Space: calm seating and clear resources. Voice: an optional response about the fictional case. Audience: an adult listens or reads and responds. Influence: record any change to the task support or next teaching step. A pass is respected and does not require an explanation.

S: reflect on a fictional person’s needs and choices. M: consider caring and helpful actions. So: listen to different possible responses. IL: respect a choice to pause or use a response aid. MR: respect different families and feelings without ranking people.

An explanation of a caring action or support-map choice may be offered to the Communication portfolio. Record the learner’s actual response about the fictional person and the adult’s reply. Staff decide any mapping.

A young person needs help with a task. A tutor listens to their question. The tutor shows one small step. This act can show care. The young person can ask once more. The tutor checks what help is wanted.

The map begins with the fictional young person who needs help to start a task. A tutor can show one step. A support adult can help ask a question or find another agreed help route. Accept one appropriate role for the core map; the second route extends the response. Do not ask for real names, family lists or contact details.

Family structure does not tell us how much care a person receives. Caring relationships can take different forms. Care is shown through actions, not appearance, gifts or an adult’s title. A young person can ask for more help if one response does not meet the need.
